q: Over an average lifetime, roughly how many times does a human heart beat?
w: ~70 beats per minute × ~79 years ≈ 2.9 billion; the commonly cited figure is 2.5–3 billion. Your heart is startlingly industrious.

q: Roughly how many piano tuners work in New York City?
w: The original Fermi estimate: NYC has ~8M people, maybe 100k pianos, tuned ~1–2× a year, each tuner doing 4–6 a day — you land around 100–200.

q: Counting all its branches, roughly how long is the Great Wall of China in kilometers?
w: A 2008 government survey of all dynasties’ sections put it at 21,196 km. The Ming-era stonework most people picture is about 8,850 km.

q: Roughly how many hairs grow on the average human head?
w: About 100,000, with blondes averaging more (~140k) and redheads fewer (~90k). Each lasts ~3 years before falling out.

q: Roughly how many cups of coffee are drunk worldwide on an average day?
w: ~2.25 billion cups a day — roughly one cup for every 3–4 humans alive, before breakfast even ends.

q: Roughly how many registered motor vehicles are there in the United States?
w: About 280 million registered vehicles — comfortably more than one per American adult. The US has been a carapaced nation since the 1970s.

q: Roughly how many books are held in the US Library of Congress?
w: ~25 million books (cataloged) out of ~170 million total items including maps, films, and recordings. The largest library on Earth.

q: What is the total weight of the Eiffel Tower, in metric tonnes?
w: About 10,100 tonnes of wrought iron — 7,300 t of it in the lattice structure alone, plus paint, elevators, and restaurants.

q: What is the mass of the International Space Station, in kilograms?
w: ~420,000 kg — a football-field-sized outpost assembled over 40+ missions and continuously crewed since November 2000.

q: At its peak around 100 CE, roughly how many people lived in the city of Rome itself?
w: Around one million — the first city in history to reach that mark. Estimates range from 800k to over a million depending on who counts as a resident.

q: Roughly how many steps would it take to walk around the Earth at the equator?
w: 40,075 km at ~0.75 m per stride ≈ 53 million steps. Water walking not included.

q: How many liters of water does an Olympic swimming pool hold?
w: 2,500 m³ = 2.5 million liters (2.5 megaliters). The standard spec: 50 m × 25 m × ~2 m deep on average.

q: Roughly how many Google searches are performed worldwide each day?
w: Commonly cited at ~8.5 billion a day — nearly one per person alive, daily. (Search is the water we swim in.)

q: Roughly how many chickens are alive on Earth at any given moment?
w: ~25 billion. Chickens are the most numerous bird in history by a wild margin — there are roughly 3 chickens per human.

q: Roughly how much gold has been mined in all of human history, in metric tonnes?
w: About 210,000 t — which would fit in a cube ~22 meters on a side. Nearly all of it mined in the last century and a half.

q: Roughly how many total words did William Shakespeare write across all his works?
w: ~884,000 words across 37+ plays and 154 sonnets — and he introduced or popularized hundreds of words still in daily use.

q: Roughly how many photographs are taken worldwide each year?
w: Estimates run to ~2 trillion a year — about half of them by smartphones, and overwhelmingly selfies adjacent to food.

q: Roughly how many babies are born worldwide on an average day?
w: ~365,000 per day — about 4 every second, which works out to ~132 million a year.

q: The Moon’s distance from Earth is about how many Earth diameters?
w: ~30 Earths would fit side by side between us and the Moon (384,400 km ÷ 12,742 km ≈ 30). It’s much farther than most diagrams suggest.

q: Roughly how many solar eclipses (total or partial) occur somewhere on Earth per century?
w: About 240 per century — roughly 2–5 per year somewhere on the planet, though any single spot waits ~375 years for a total eclipse.

q: Roughly how many pizzas are sold in the United States per year?
w: ~3 billion a year — about 350 slices per second. Americans eat roughly 23 pounds of pizza per person annually.

q: Roughly how many liters of water does Lake Superior contain?
w: ~12,100 km³ = about 1.2 × 10¹⁶ liters — enough to cover North and South America in a foot of water. It holds 10% of the world’s surface freshwater.

q: Roughly how many neurons are in a human brain?
w: The commonly cited figure is ~86 billion neurons (Azevedo et al., 2009) — about as many stars as a mid-size galaxy holds.

q: Roughly how many steps does the average walker cover in a mile?
w: The classic planning figure is ~2,000 steps per mile — roughly 2.5 feet per stride. An active adult wanders about 5 miles a day.

q: Roughly how many items does the Library of Congress hold?
w: The commonly cited total is ~170 million items — books, maps, photographs, recordings, and everything else crammed into the stacks.

q: Roughly how many living cells make up a human body?
w: Recent estimates put it around 37 trillion (Bianconi et al., 2013); older textbooks waved at 10–100 trillion. You are a walking census.

q: Roughly how many airline passengers flew worldwide in 2019?
w: About 4.5 billion scheduled passengers (IATA) — more than half of humanity aloft in a single year, before the skies went quiet.

q: Roughly how many words are in current use in English?
w: The OED counts ~170,000 words in current use — a fraction of the 600,000+ headwords it has catalogued. Shakespeare got by with about 30,000.

q: Roughly how many bones are in an adult human skeleton?
w: 206 after growth finishes, down from about 270 at birth as plates fuse. The smallest, the stapes in the middle ear, is the size of a grain of rice.

q: Roughly how many seconds does sunlight take to reach Earth?
w: About 499 seconds on average, a shade over eight minutes. The Sun you see outside is always eight minutes out of date.

q: Roughly how many humans have ever lived?
w: About 117 billion births by the usual demographic estimate, against 8 billion alive today. For every living person, roughly fourteen have gone before.

q: Roughly how fast does the International Space Station travel, in kilometers per hour?
w: About 28,000 km/h, or 7.7 kilometers every second. The crew watches a sunrise about every 90 minutes.

q: Roughly how many stars can a dark, clear night show to the naked eye, counting both hemispheres?
w: A few thousand per sky at a truly dark site, around 6,000 in total across both hemispheres on a perfect night. Every single one belongs to our own galaxy.

q: Roughly how many people have reached the summit of Mount Everest?
w: Somewhere past 6,000 summiteers by recent counts, several of them multiple times, against a death toll in the low hundreds. The summit queue is a modern invention.

q: Roughly how many barrels of oil does the world consume each day?
w: On the close order of 100 million barrels a day. Spread across humanity, that is about 12 liters each per day, a number most people prefer not to picture.

q: Roughly how fast does the ground move at the equator, in kilometers per hour?
w: About 1,670 km/h, one full lap a day. You are standing on a carousel that never slows, and you have never felt a thing.

q: Roughly how many stars are in the Milky Way galaxy?
w: Estimates run from 100 to 400 billion; 250 billion sits mid-field. To count them aloud at one per second would take nearly 8,000 years.

q: Roughly how many times does a person blink in a waking day?
w: Around 15 blinks a minute across 16 waking hours is about 14,000 to 19,000 a day. Your eyes are closed for a cumulative hour and a half without your ever leaving the room.

q: Roughly how many words does an average person speak in a day?
w: Studies that tape whole days of talk land between 10,000 and 20,000 words, averaging near 16,000. Some days you talk like a novella and some like a telegram.

q: Roughly how many days long is an average human lifetime?
w: Seventy-nine years times 365 days is about 28,800; round it to 29,000. Put that way, a whole life is small enough to count on a calendar page.

q: Roughly how many aircraft are airborne over the Earth at this moment?
w: Flight trackers watch roughly 9,000 to 11,000 planes aloft at a busy moment, day or night. A small city hangs overhead around the clock.

q: Roughly how many emails are sent worldwide each day?
w: The count is around 350 billion a day, and the great majority of it is spam. Nine in ten messages flying around the world right now are junk written by machines for machines.

q: Roughly how many passenger cars are there on Earth?
w: A bit over 1.4 billion vehicles are registered worldwide, most of them cars. Parked nose to tail, they would circle the equator a hundred times over.

q: Roughly how many trees are there on Earth?
w: A satellite-era census published in Nature put the figure near 3 trillion, roughly eight times the old textbook guess. Humanity fells some 15 billion a year, so the arithmetic is not on our side.

q: Roughly how deep is the deepest point of the ocean, in meters?
w: Challenger Deep runs about 10,900 to 11,000 meters down. Drop Mount Everest into it and the summit would still sit two kilometers below the waves.

q: Roughly how many people live in greater Tokyo?
w: The metropolitan web of commuting rails holds about 37 million people, the largest urban area on Earth. Greater Tokyo alone would out-populate most of the world’s countries.
